articles.headline: OFAC Issues Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations, Amends Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. This action underscores the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to combat global illicit networks.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License to ensure legitimate humanitarian and other authorized activities are not unduly impacted. Additionally, an amended Russia-related General License was published, alongside updated Frequently Asked Questions, indicating adjustments to existing sanctions on Russia.
These measures reflect a continued focus on disrupting criminal enterprises while also refining sanctions programs to address evolving geopolitical landscapes and minimize unintended consequences.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations under its counter terrorism authority. These actions aim to disrupt the financial and material support networks of terrorist organizations globally.

The specific individuals and entities targeted were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement, but such designations typically involve freezing assets and prohibiting transactions with U.S. persons.
These measures are part of a broader strategy to safeguard the U.S. financial system from exploitation by terrorist groups and their facilitators.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Narcotics and Terrorism Networks with New Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced a dual set of designations, targeting both counter narcotics and counter terrorism networks. This action highlights the interconnectedness of various illicit activities and the U.S. government's comprehensive approach to combating them.
The designations aim to disrupt the financial flows and operational capabilities of individuals and entities involved in drug trafficking and supporting terrorist organizations.
Further details on the specific targets and the implications of these designations are expected to be released, reinforcing the U.S. commitment to global security.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designations, Reinforcing Sanctions Regime
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an update to its Iran designations, signaling continued pressure on the Iranian regime and its associated networks. This action follows previous measures aimed at restricting Iran's access to the international financial system.

While specific details of the updated designations were not immediately available, such actions typically involve adding individuals and entities to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List, thereby blocking their assets and prohibiting transactions with U.S. persons.
These ongoing designation updates are part of the U.S. government's broader strategy to counter Iran's destabilizing activities in the region and its nuclear program.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations Targeting Digital Asset Sector
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations, specifically targeting eight Canada-based money services businesses. These entities are accused of operating in the digital asset sector of the Iranian economy.

According to OFAC, these businesses have been involved in exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets, with many reportedly dealing with sanctioned Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

This action, coordinated with FinCEN, Canada's financial intelligence unit, and the Drug Enforcement Administration, highlights the U.S. government's focus on preventing the use of digital assets for sanctions evasion and illicit finance by Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Issues Cuba-related Determination
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced a series of designations targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations. This action aims to disrupt illicit financial activities and cyber-enabled fraud networks globally.
In a separate but related action, OFAC also issued new Cuba designations, adding two individuals, six entities, and two vessels to the SDN List under E.O. 14404.
Furthermore, OFAC published a Cuba-related determination, providing additional guidance and clarity regarding the scope of sanctions on Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-related Designations, Amends Venezuela-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations, targeting four individuals and nine entities allegedly linked to an India-based network supporting Iran's shadow fleet. This network is accused of providing false flags and certifications to sanctioned vessels involved in transporting Iranian petroleum.

Concurrently, OFAC issued an alert warning maritime service providers of designation and penalty risks associated with vessels using false flags to evade Iran sanctions, encouraging enhanced due diligence.

Additionally, OFAC issued Venezuela General License 5AA, replacing General License 5Z and postponing until December 18, 2026, the authorization for specified transactions involving the PDVSA 2020 8.5 percent bond.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment aims to clarify or adjust existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are issued to permit specific types of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs, often to facilitate humanitarian aid, personal remittances, or other authorized activities.
The details of the amendments will be crucial for entities and individuals engaged in permissible activities with Iran, as they outline the scope and limitations of the authorized transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Sanctions on North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo Entities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations targeting entities related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions are part of ongoing efforts to address threats to international security and human rights.
The North Korea designations likely aim to disrupt the regime's illicit financing activities and its weapons of mass destruction programs.
The DRC-related designations are expected to target individuals or entities involved in corruption, human rights abuses, or destabilizing activities within the region.

Settlement agreements typically involve a company agreeing to pay a monetary penalty and implement remedial measures to enhance their compliance programs.
This action underscores OFAC's continued enforcement of sanctions laws and the importance for companies to maintain robust compliance frameworks to prevent violations.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 in OFAC Settlement
body: Bank of America, N.A. has settled with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $11,662,930 due to 475 apparent sanctions violations. These violations covered numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

This settlement was part of a coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC for anti-money laundering and sanctions failures.

The bank admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain an adequate AML program, conduct due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts, and file Suspicious Activity Reports in a timely manner.

articles.headline: Central Banks Signal Further Tightening Amidst Inflation Concerns
body: The American Federal Reserve is considering new rate hikes to bring inflation back to its 2% target, with minutes from their October 27 and 28 meeting indicating that nearly all participants felt further hikes might be necessary.

Similarly, the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of England (BoE) have also signaled additional monetary tightening. The BoE, in its November Monetary Policy Report, noted that the conflict in the Middle East is in its ninth month and global energy prices have continued to rise.

This hawkish stance from major central banks comes despite signs of easing in energy markets, with wholesale gasoline futures losing nearly 20% in three weeks and average U.S. retail gasoline prices dropping by 12.8% in one month.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Decline Amidst Surplus Conditions, Middle East Disruptions Persist
body: Brent crude declined 1.5% to close at $92.0/bbl on November 19, as recent data suggest the oil market is experiencing surplus conditions. This decline follows a period of rising energy costs, partly fueled by the war with Iran which began in March 2026.

Despite the overall decline, Middle East disruptions continue to constrain energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, sustaining upside risks to prices. The U.S. Maritime Administration has acknowledged the naval blockade's impact on insurance premiums and cargo capacity in the Gulf.
Meanwhile, TTF gas prices fell sharply due to a notable increase in LNG supply flows into Europe, as large tankers have rerouted towards the continent in recent days.

articles.headline: Iran Fires Drones at U.S. Military Radar System in Bahrain
body: Iran today fired drones at a U.S. military radar system located at the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed responsibility for the attack.
Bahrain reported that it intercepted the attack, and there were no immediate reports of casualties or damage. This incident marks a significant escalation in regional tensions.

New U.S. intelligence also indicates that Iran is developing plans to target senior officials in the Trump administration with a 'dirty bomb' or chemical weapon in Washington D.C., though officials characterized this as an option rather than an imminent threat.

articles.headline: Ukraine Damages Crimea Bridge in 'Unprecedented Operation,' Russia Retaliates
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed an 'unprecedented operation' after Ukraine severely damaged the bridge linking Russia to Crimea. Images shared by Ukrainian officials showed a section of the Kerch Bridge collapsed in the water.

In retaliation, Russia reportedly carried out its largest drone strike of the war so far, according to Moscow, damaging the major bridge connecting Russia with occupied Crimea and striking several oil refineries.
Kyiv experienced 17 air raid alerts in one day, the most on record, and Russian strikes killed at least seven people in Ukraine, leaving 50,000 without power due to attacks on energy infrastructure.

articles.headline: Escalating Violence in Gaza and West Bank Amidst Failed Ceasefire Commitments

In the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials and witnesses reported that Israeli militant settlers killed a 72-year-old woman overnight in Jericho, where settlers recently took over several Palestinian homes.

These killings come as Israel has failed to meet its aid commitments under the Gaza ceasefire deal, with data showing decreasing food deliveries and severe shortages of medical supplies, tents, and materials for infrastructure repair.

articles.headline: OCC Fines Bank of America $750 Million for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) imposed a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. for its deficient and ineffective Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program. This represents the largest civil money penalty in the OCC's history.

The OCC's action follows a December 2024 cease-and-desist order, indicating that more than a year later, the bank still failed to escalate potentially suspicious activity for investigation and processed potential trade-based money laundering due to a transaction-monitoring gap.
This penalty was credited toward the $1.2 billion penalty assessed by the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) against Bank of America for related failures.
articles.source: Lewis Baach Kaufmann Middlemiss / ACAMS / FinCEN

articles.headline: BIS Expands Export Controls on Advanced Computing, Targets Remote Access and Data Centers
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule (IFR) on November 16, 2026, which took effect upon publication in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026. This rule significantly expands export controls on advanced computing items, including advanced semiconductors and certain foreign data center activities involving remote access to computing power.

The IFR establishes new end-use controls requiring a license for the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of advanced computing items if there is 'knowledge' that they will be used in a data center providing significant computing power to an entity headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent is headquartered in, Macau or a Country Group D:5 country (including China).

Additionally, the rule adds a new destination-based license requirement for advanced computing items to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, citing concerns about diversion risks. Data centers already providing significant compute to D:5/Macau-headquartered companies before publication must obtain a license within 90 days.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Federal Register / Gibson Dunn

articles.headline: BIS Renews Rossiya Airlines' Temporary Denial Order for One Year

The denial order continues to restrict transactions involving covered items and services for the airline, though it remains subject to BIS-authorized safety-of-flight exceptions.

This action underscores BIS's commitment to enforcing export controls against entities that undermine U.S. national security and foreign policy interests, particularly in the context of ongoing sanctions against Russia.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Federal Register

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of Affiliates Rule Until January 2027
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced an extension of the suspension of its Affiliates Rule until January 10, 2027. This extension, effective November 9, 2026, further stays amendments to 15 CFR parts 732, 734, 736, 744, and 748.
The Affiliates Rule pertains to end-user controls and its suspension provides continued flexibility for certain transactions involving affiliates of listed entities.
This decision indicates BIS's ongoing evaluation of the rule's impact and its commitment to providing clarity and stability for businesses navigating export control regulations.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Federal Register

articles.headline: UFLPA Entity List Expanded with 43 New Chinese Entities
body: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, chair of the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force (FLETF), announced the largest expansion of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List in history, adding 43 new Chinese companies. This brings the total number of entities on the list to 187.

Four of the newly added entities were listed for working with the government of Xinjiang to recruit, transport, transfer, harbor, or receive forced labor or members of persecuted groups out of Xinjiang. An additional 41 entities were added for sourcing material from the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region (XUAR) or from persons working with the Xinjiang government or the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps (XPCC) for forced labor programs.

Effective October 29, goods produced by three affiliated Chinese companies, identified as one of the largest advanced gene-sequencing and genetic-material collection enterprises, were also prohibited from entering the U.S. for helping the Xinjiang government build and operate its mass surveillance infrastructure.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
